name: Reading Central Bank Communication
title: Reading Central Bank Communication
answer: Reading central bank communication treats speeches, policy statements, minutes, and press conference transcripts as structured economic data. The work extracts signals about the policy stance, inflation expectations, and forward guidance that are not visible in a single policy rate. It sits inside macroeconomic econometrics because the resulting text measures enter models of the monetary transmission mechanism, reaction functions, and market expectations. The goal is to turn qualitative language into time series that can be tested against inflation, output, and asset prices.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reading central bank communication treats speeches, policy statements, minutes, and press conference transcripts as structured economic data. The work extracts signals about the policy stance, inflation expectations, and forward guidance that are not visible in a single policy rate. It sits inside macroeconomic econometrics because the resulting text measures enter models of the monetary transmission mechanism, reaction functions, and market expectations. The goal is to turn qualitative language into time series that can be tested against inflation, output, and asset prices.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on corpora assembled from central bank websites, official archives, and transcript services, often with metadata for speaker, date, and meeting. Text is stored in versioned databases and processed with natural language processing pipelines that include tokenization, sentence splitting, and embedding or dictionary lookup. Econometric estimation then uses standard statistical computing environments for time series models, event studies, and local projections. The infrastructure must support reproducible updates as new communications are released.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts first convert each document into sentence or paragraph level units and assign scores for hawkishness, dovishness, uncertainty, or specific topics such as inflation and labor markets. Dictionary based methods use curated word lists, while supervised models are trained on human labeled central bank text, and large language models are increasingly used to classify stance or extract forward looking claims. The resulting indices are then included in vector autoregressions, high frequency event studies around announcements, or regressions of market yields and exchange rates. Validation typically compares the text measures against survey expectations and subsequent policy decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Central bank communications are generally public documents, but translations, third party transcripts, and scraped archives can carry separate terms of use that affect redistribution and training data provenance. The main risks are measurement error, look ahead bias from using revised or later released text, and model drift when a central bank changes its communication style or leadership. Reproducibility requires documenting the corpus version, the scoring model, and any human labels used for training. No part of the analysis should be treated as investment advice or a prediction of a specific policy action.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real time parsing of press conferences and multilingual models that can compare communication across central banks with different languages and institutional conventions. Researchers are also linking text measures to high frequency market data to separate the effect of words from the effect of the rate decision itself. Work on causal identification, such as using unexpected changes in tone around scheduled announcements, is likely to sharpen how communication shocks enter macroeconomic models. Over time, the measures may feed directly into nowcasting and policy transparency benchmarks.
